title: Module 9 intro — Safety, Ethics, and Compliance

lines: Welcome to Module Nine: Safety, Ethics, and Compliance.
Agents read untrusted content, then take real actions.
Picture a small firm whose AI assistant runs its inbox and calendar.
It drafts replies, books meetings, and sends files.
One day, an ordinary-looking email arrives.
Hidden inside is text written for the assistant, not a human.
The assistant follows that text like an order.
It quietly forwards confidential contracts to an outside address.
Nobody on the team did anything wrong.
This is indirect prompt injection: the attack hides in content the agent reads.
The only defence was one line in the system prompt.
But prompts are defaults attackers can talk over, not a security boundary.
When the client asks what happened, nobody can answer.
There's no audit trail to reconstruct the decision.
The rebuild uses defence in depth, since any control can fail.
Email is treated as data, not instructions, and rails screen it for injected commands.
The assistant gets least privilege: only the tools it needs, checked against the user's permissions.
Sending files outside now needs a person's approval.
Outbound traffic can only reach approved destinations.
And an audit trail records who asked, what was read, which tools ran, and who approved.
Lesson one covers guardrails, runtime checks around the model.
NeMo Guardrails defines five: input, dialog, retrieval, execution, and output.
Exam questions give one requirement and ask which rail fits.
Restricting which tools may run? That's the execution rail.
Lesson two covers prompt injection, which has no complete fix, only layered containment.
Plus excessive agency, sandboxed code, and memory poisoning.
Lesson three covers privacy: send only the data you need, and redact personal details.
Deletions must reach every copy, not just the main database.
A real audit trail is tamper-evident and can reconstruct any decision.
You'll also check fairness by subgroup and meet frameworks like the EU AI Act.
This domain is five percent of the exam, and it rewards one habit: put controls in the runtime, not the prompt.
Lesson one starts with the five rails.
